Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Carlos, a 62-year-old dancer, had spent decades moving gracefully across stages, each performance a celebration of life and artistry. But everything changed one fateful afternoon in October when he was involved in a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. The accident, a sudden and violent event, had left him with physical injuries that healed over time, but the psychological scars ran much deeper. It was a sunny day, and Carlos had been driving home after a rehearsal, feeling a sense of joy and anticipation about an upcoming performance. In an instant, a speeding car collided with his, the impact shattering the quiet of the day. He remembered the sound of metal crunching, the smell of smoke and gasoline, and the weight of fear as he realized the precariousness of life. 

In the months that followed, Carlos found himself grappling with an emotional fallout that he couldn't quite articulate. He often felt disconnected from his own body, as if watching his life unfold from a distance. Deliberately, he would try to leave his body or blank out during moments of overwhelming stress, hoping to escape the rawness of his emotions. Sleep eluded him, too; he would stay up late into the night, the darkness a companion that he could control. Thoughts of the accident clawed at him, and he tried hard not to think about it, suppressing the memories that threatened to invade his mind like uninvited guests.

As time passed, Carlos became increasingly vigilant, scanning for exits as soon as he entered any room, a habit born out of an acute awareness of danger that had seeped into his daily life. He felt a growing sense of dread, accompanied by strong negative emotions that twisted his stomach into knots. Fear, anger, and guilt churned within him, but he often felt ashamed to admit these feelings, believing they were a betrayal of the resilient persona he had always projected. When he was unexpectedly touched by someone, he would startle, an involuntary reaction that left him embarrassed and frustrated. It was as if he were continually trapped in a state of hyper-vigilance, unable to shake the feeling that danger lurked around every corner.

Carlos struggled with his memories, too. The details of the accident were often elusive, slipping through his fingers like sand. He found it challenging to put the frightening event into words, instead experiencing it as a series of vivid, disjointed images accompanied by auditory echoes of the crash—screeching tires, shattering glass, and the chaos that ensued. Each recollection was tinged with an intense sense of shame, as if the very act of remembering was a confession of his perceived weakness.

What frightened Carlos most was the belief that he would never be able to experience normal emotions again. He felt lost in a haze of helplessness, convinced that he could do nothing to prevent bad things from happening to him. He couldn't shake the thought that the accident had occurred because of the kind of person he believed himself to be—a dancer who had always embraced life with fervor but now felt like a shadow of his former self. This self-blame compounded his suffering, isolating him further from the joy he once derived from his art.

Relationships began to shift as Carlos withdrew from his family and friends. He avoided social gatherings, fearing the vulnerability of being around others who might inadvertently trigger memories he was desperate to avoid. His wife, Elena, noticed the change in him, the way he seemed distant and preoccupied, his laughter replaced by silence. She tried to reach out, but Carlos often brushed her off, too ashamed to share the turmoil that raged within him. 

It was this growing sense of isolation and the realization that he could no longer dance without feeling the weight of his trauma that finally brought Carlos to seek help. He was terrified of what lay ahead—of facing the memories head-on, of stripping away the façade he had built to protect himself. But deep down, he hoped for a return to the man he once was, one who could embrace life fully and find joy in both dance and relationships once more.
